title: Hanging a wooden shed door with tee hinges
subtitle: Fit and hang a ledge-and-brace shed door using tee hinges on a timber door frame, plumbing the door and adjusting for a close fit
excerpt: How to hang a ledge-and-brace shed door on tee hinges. Covers fitting the hinges to the door, plumbing the frame, hanging the door, and fitting a latch and a hasp.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Carpentry for Boys (1914, public domain). Collins DIY Guide (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A T-shaped strap hinge in which the long arm (the strap) screws to the door face and the short arm (the knuckle section) screws to the door frame. Used for ledge-and-brace shed, garage, and garden-gate doors. Available in 150 mm, 200 mm, 250 mm, and 300 mm strap lengths; use the longest that suits the door size.

A simple door construction used for sheds and outbuildings: vertical boards nailed to two or three horizontal ledges, with diagonal braces running from the lower hinge side to the upper latch side to prevent the door from drooping. The brace must run upward toward the hinge side to work correctly.

content.text: screwed to the door face and the frame. The job is fit the hinges, hang the door with a temporary packing piece under the bottom edge, and adjust the fit. A door that is plumb and true when first hung saves years of subsequent sticking and adjustment.

Check that the door is square by measuring diagonals; they must be equal. If the door is slightly racked, knock the hinge-side bottom corner away from the latch side while the ledges are still firm. Check that the door is 3-5 mm narrower than the opening all round. Plane down any face that is too close with a block plane or a jack plane.
Fix the hinges to the door

Lay the door flat. Position the top hinge 200 mm from the top of the door, aligned with the top ledge. Position the bottom hinge 200 mm from the bottom, aligned with the bottom ledge. Screw the long strap of each hinge to the door face (the full length of the strap, at least four screws per strap, into the ledges). Do not countersink tee-hinge screws: the round-head screws are driven flush to the surface.

Prop the door in the opening with a packing piece (a couple of tiles or a folded piece of board) under the bottom edge to hold the door at the correct height. Align the hinge knuckle sections against the frame face. Check the door is plumb with a spirit level on the hinge stile. Mark the hinge positions on the frame through the knuckle holes. Remove the door, drill pilot holes in the frame, refit the door, and screw the knuckle to the frame.

A simple Suffolk-type latch (thumb latch) or a hasp and padlock is the standard shed door furniture. Fit the latch plate to the frame and the lever arm to the door, adjusting the height so the lever sits horizontally in the closed position. Fit the hasp to the door face and the staple to the frame for a padlock.

attrs.symptom: The door drops and drags on the sill after a few months
attrs.cause: The brace was fitted running the wrong way (hinge side to top, latch side to bottom) or was not fixed tightly.
attrs.fix: The brace must run from the bottom of the hinge stile to the top of the latch stile. Re-nail or re-screw the brace in the correct direction.

attrs.symptom: Door sticks or binds on the frame during summer
attrs.cause: Timber swelling with moisture in warm, wet weather.
attrs.fix: Plane the binding edge back by 2-3 mm and treat with a timber preservative. A shed door in an exposed position needs the edges primed or treated as well as the faces.
